9.4 Why Do Objects Float or Sink in Water?

You must have observed that some objects float while others sink in water (Fig. 9.9). You may have noticed that, while washing rice, husk particles present in the rice float on the surface of water while rice sinks to the bottom of the container. Why does this happen? If you add oil to water, it floats on water. Generally, it is believed that objects that float in a liquid are lighter and others that sink are heavier than the liquid. A wooden stick and an iron rod may be of the same size, yet the iron rod feels much heavier. When we say that iron is heavier than wood, we are referring to a special property known as density, which describes the heaviness of an object. Note However, the density of a substance is not the only factor that decides whether it will float or sink in a particular liquid. Let us explore further.
9.5 What Is Density?

Imagine a crowded bus where many people are packed together — this is an example of high density whereas, the same bus with only a few people is an example of low density. Similarly, a forest where trees grow close to each other is called a dense forest (Fig.  9.10a), but if the trees are far apart (Fig. 9.10b), it is considered less dense. How do scientists define density? Let us find out. We have learnt that matter is anything that possesses mass and occupies space (volume). Density is defined as the mass present in a unit volume of that substance. The density of a substance may be expressed mathematically using the formula: Density = MassVolume The density of a substance is independent of its shape or size. However, it is dependent on temperature and pressure. Pressure primarily affects the density of gases, while its effect on solids and liquids is negligible.

As you have learnt, the SI units of mass and volume are kilogram ( kg) and cubic metre ( m3), respectively. Therefore, the SI unit of density is kilogram per cubic metre, abbreviated as kg/m3. Let us dig deeper! Did you know that our planet, Earth, is composed of several layers, such as crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core, and inner core, each with its particular range of density? In ancient times, before large ships were invented, people used bamboo and wooden logs to travel across rivers and seas (Fig. 9.21). Bamboo was used because it is light, hollow, and floats easily on water. People tied bamboo poles together to make rafts and small boats for fishing, trading, and crossing water bodies. Wooden logs, especially from strong trees were either hollowed out to make boats or used as rafts. These simple boats, made from locally available materials, were important for moving around and connecting different places. 9.5.2 Effect of temperature on density

Generally, the density of a substance decreases with heating and increases with cooling. This can be explained on the basis of what you have learnt in chapter ‘Particulate Nature of Matter’. As temperature increases, the particles of a substance whether, solid, liquid, or gas, tend to move away and spread. This results in an increase in volume but there is no change in mass. Since the Density = Mass/Volume, upon heating, the volume increases and the density decreases. This explains why hot air moves up as it is less dense than the cool air around it. The hot air balloon works on the same principle (Fig. 9.22).

9.5.3 Effect of pressure on density

Pressure affects density differently depending on the state of matter. For gases, increasing pressure causes the particles to move closer together. As a result, the volume of the gas decreases and its density increases. In the case of liquids, pressure has a small effect because they are nearly incompressible. We have learnt in chapter ‘Particulate Nature of Matter’ that the particles in solids are very close to each other. So, how is the density of solids affected when pressure is applied? Solids are even less affected by pressure than liquids, and changes in their density are usually negligible.
Ever heard of ...

Why does ice float on water? Ice floats on water because it is lighter than liquid water (Fig. 9.23). Water has a special property that its density is highest at 4 °C. As the temperature drops, and water turns into ice at 0 °C, it undergoes a change in structure—the particles arrange themselves in a way that takes up more space. This process is called expansion. Because the same amount of water now occupies a larger volume, its density decreases. As a result, ice becomes lighter than liquid water and floats on its surface. This is important for animals living in lakes and oceans because ice floats, it forms a layer on top, keeping the water underneath warm enough for fish and other creatures to survive, even in extremely cold weather.

Our scientific heritage

Ningel village in Manipur’s Thoubal district is a place where salt is still produced using traditional methods. The village has a few salt wells, one of which is lined with a 100-year-old tree trunk placed into the ground to draw up salty water. A few families mostly women, continue this sacred practice by collecting the salt solution and boiling it in large metal pans over firewood kilns. Once the water evaporates and salt crystals form, they are shaped into round ‘salt cakes’ using banana leaves and handmade tools. These cakes are then wrapped in a traditional cloth (phanek) to protect them. The salt cakes are believed to have some medicinal value too. ask_qa.q: Why do sugar and salt dissolve in water but not in oil?
ask_qa.a: Water is a very good solvent because of its chemical nature, which allows it to attract and break apart the particles of salt and sugar. Oil has a different structure that doesn't interact with salt or sugar in the same way.

ask_qa.q: Does stirring a solution make more solute dissolve?
ask_qa.a: Stirring only helps the solute dissolve faster by bringing fresh solvent into contact with the solute. It does not change the actual solubility limit of the liquid.

ask_qa.q: If I break a stone in half, does its density change?
ask_qa.a: No, the density remains the same. Even though the mass and volume both decrease, the ratio of mass to volume stays constant for the same material.

ask_qa.q: How can I make a saturated solution dissolve more solute without adding more water?
ask_qa.a: You can increase the temperature of the solution. For most solid solutes, heating the solvent increases its capacity to hold more solute.

ask_qa.q: What is the displacement method?
ask_qa.a: It is a way to find the volume of an irregular object by submerged it in a measuring cylinder filled with water. The increase in the water level equals the volume of the object.

ask_qa.q: Why is 'Relative Density' a number without any units?
ask_qa.a: Because it is a ratio of two densities (Density of substance / Density of water), the units cancel each other out.

ask_qa.q: How does pressure affect the density of a solid?
ask_qa.a: Pressure has a negligible effect on the density of solids because their particles are already packed very closely together and cannot be compressed much.

ask_qa.q: Why do some oranges sink when peeled but float when unpeeled?
ask_qa.a: The peel of an orange contains tiny air pockets that act like a life jacket, decreasing the overall density of the fruit. Removing the peel removes these air pockets, making the orange denser than water.

ask_qa.q: What is a solution?
ask_qa.a: A solution is a uniform mixture of a solute and a solvent where the components are evenly distributed.

ask_qa.q: What is a solute?
ask_qa.a: A solute is the part of a solution that gets dissolved, usually present in a smaller amount.

ask_qa.q: What is a solvent?
ask_qa.a: A solvent is the substance that does the dissolving, typically present in a larger amount in a solution.

ask_qa.q: How can you identify the solute in a liquid-liquid solution?
ask_qa.a: In a mixture of two liquids, the substance present in the smaller amount is called the solute.

ask_qa.q: Define a uniform mixture.
ask_qa.a: A uniform mixture is one where the components are evenly distributed throughout, making it look the same everywhere, like salt water.

ask_qa.q: What is a non-uniform mixture?
ask_qa.a: A non-uniform mixture is one where the components are not evenly distributed and can often be seen separately, like sand in water.

ask_qa.q: What happens when you add too much salt to water and it stops dissolving?
ask_qa.a: The solution becomes saturated, and the extra salt settles at the bottom of the container.

ask_qa.q: What is a saturated solution?
ask_qa.a: A saturated solution is a solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at that specific temperature.

ask_qa.q: What is an unsaturated solution?
ask_qa.a: An unsaturated solution is one where more solute can still be dissolved at the current temperature.

ask_qa.q: How does temperature affect the solubility of solids like sugar or salt?
ask_qa.a: For most solids, solubility increases as the temperature of the solvent increases.

ask_qa.q: What is solubility?
ask_qa.a: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a fixed quantity of solvent at a particular temperature.

ask_qa.q: Does sugar dissolve in oil?
ask_qa.a: No, sugar and salt dissolve in water but generally do not dissolve in oil because of their different chemical structures.

ask_qa.q: How can you make a saturated solution dissolve more solute without adding more water?
ask_qa.a: You can heat the solution, as increasing the temperature usually increases the solubility of solid solutes.

ask_qa.q: What is the relation between solubility of gases and temperature?

ask_qa.q: What are common units for density in a lab?
ask_qa.a: Commonly used units include grams per millilitre (g/mL) or grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³).

ask_qa.q: What is relative density?

ask_qa.q: What is a meniscus?

ask_qa.q: What is mass?

ask_qa.q: What is weight?

ask_qa.q: Why does ice float on water?

ask_qa.a: A dense forest has many trees packed closely together, while a less dense forest has trees spaced far apart.

ask_qa.q: Why does a peeled orange sink but an unpeeled orange float?

ask_qa.q: Why was bamboo used to make traditional rafts?

ask_qa.q: What is the volume of a liquid if 1 mL = 1 cm³?
ask_qa.a: The volume is the same; 1 millilitre is equivalent to 1 cubic centimetre (1 cc).

ask_qa.q: What is ORS and why is it uniform?
ask_qa.a: Oral Rehydration Solution is a mixture of salt, sugar, and water; it is uniform because the components are evenly distributed.

ask_qa.q: What happens to the density of the Earth's layers as you go deeper?

ask_qa.q: Give examples of non-uniform mixtures mentioned in the chapter.
ask_qa.a: Chalk powder in water, sand in water, and sawdust in water are examples of non-uniform mixtures because the components are not evenly distributed.

ask_qa.q: Give an example of a solution where the solvent is a liquid but the solute is a gas.
ask_qa.a: Oxygen gas dissolved in water is a common example, which is vital for the survival of aquatic life like fish and plants.

ask_qa.a: When mixing two liquids, the substance present in the smaller quantity is called the solute, while the one in the larger quantity is the solvent.

ask_qa.q: What is the Chashni (sugar syrup) example from the chapter?
ask_qa.a: In Gulab jamun syrup, a large amount of sugar is dissolved in a small amount of water; surprisingly, water is still the solvent and sugar is the solute.

ask_qa.q: Compare the concentration of 2 spoons of salt in 100 mL of water versus 4 spoons of salt in 50 mL of water.

ask_qa.q: What happens to undissolved baking soda in a saturated solution when it is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C?
ask_qa.a: The undissolved baking soda will dissolve because the increase in temperature increases the solubility of the substance in water.

ask_qa.q: Why is cold water better for aquatic species than warm water?
ask_qa.a: Solubility of gases decreases as temperature increases, so cold water holds more dissolved oxygen for fish and plants to breathe than warm water.

ask_qa.q: If you add oil to water, why does it float?
ask_qa.a: Oil floats because it is less dense than water. Objects that are less dense than the liquid they are placed in will always float.

ask_qa.a: Density is calculated as Mass divided by Volume (Density = Mass / Volume).

ask_qa.q: Calculate the density of an aluminium block with a mass of 27 g and a volume of 10 cm³.
ask_qa.a: The density is 27 g / 10 cm³ = 2.7 g/cm³.

ask_qa.q: If a substance has a relative density of 2.7, what does that mean?
ask_qa.a: It means the substance is 2.7 times denser than water. Relative density is a pure number without any units.

ask_qa.q: What is the approximate mass of 100 mL of water at room temperature?
ask_qa.a: Since the density of water is roughly 1 g/mL, 100 mL of water has a mass of approximately 100 g.

ask_qa.q: How do you 'tare' a digital weighing balance?
ask_qa.a: You press the tare or reset button to bring the reading back to zero, which allows you to measure the mass of an object without including the weight of its container.

ask_qa.q: How do you find the volume of a notebook with length 25 cm, width 18 cm, and height 2 cm?
ask_qa.a: Using the formula Volume = l × w × h, the volume is 25 × 18 × 2 = 900 cm³.

ask_qa.a: Subtract the initial volume of water in a cylinder (A) from the final volume after the stone is submerged (B). The volume of the stone is (B - A).

ask_qa.q: If a stone displaces 5 mL of water, what is its volume in cm³?
ask_qa.a: The volume is 5 cm³, as 1 mL is equivalent to 1 cm³ (also called 1 cc).

ask_qa.q: An object has a mass of 400 g and a volume of 40 cm³. What is its density?
ask_qa.a: The density is 400 g / 40 cm³ = 10 g/cm³.

ask_qa.a: Object A has a density of 5 g/cm³ (200/40), and Object B has a density of 4 g/cm³ (240/60). Therefore, Object A is denser.

ask_qa.q: If you have 120 g of clay and change its shape from a cube to a thin sheet, what happens to its density?
ask_qa.a: The density remains the same because the mass and total volume of the clay have not changed; density is independent of shape.

ask_qa.q: A block of iron has a mass of 600 g and a density of 7.9 g/cm³. Calculate its volume.
ask_qa.a: Using Volume = Mass / Density, the volume is 600 g / 7.9 g/cm³ ≈ 75.95 cm³.

ask_qa.q: What happens to the level of water in a tube if the air inside the test tube is heated?
ask_qa.a: The water level rises because heating the air causes it to expand (increase in volume), which makes the air less dense and causes it to move or push the liquid.

ask_qa.q: Why does a hot air balloon rise?
ask_qa.a: Heating the air inside the balloon increases its volume and decreases its density. The hot air becomes less dense than the cool air outside, causing it to move up.

ask_qa.q: What is the real-life application of bamboo's density in history?
ask_qa.a: Ancient people used bamboo to make rafts because it is light, hollow, and floats easily on water due to its low density.

ask_qa.q: Why does ice float on water according to the chapter?
ask_qa.a: When water freezes at 0 °C, it expands and occupies more space. This increased volume makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

ask_qa.a: They are used to measure specific amounts of liquids (like 50 mL or 100 mL) and to determine the volume of irregular solids like stones or metal keys.

ask_qa.q: What is the science behind why a peeled orange sinks while an unpeeled one floats?
ask_qa.a: The peel contains tiny air pockets that act like a life jacket, reducing the overall density. Removing the peel removes the air pockets, making the orange denser than water.

ask_qa.q: How can you make a raw egg float in tap water?
ask_qa.a: You can add salt to the water. This increases the density of the water until it is higher than the egg's density, causing the egg to float.

ask_qa.q: Is it true that adding more salt will eventually make it stop dissolving in water?
ask_qa.a: Yes, this is true. When a solution reaches its limit at a certain temperature and can no longer dissolve any more solute, it becomes a 'saturated' solution and the extra salt settles at the bottom.

ask_qa.q: What is the main difference between a uniform mixture and a non-uniform mixture?
ask_qa.a: In a uniform mixture (solution), components are evenly distributed and look the same throughout, like salt in water. In a non-uniform mixture, components are not even and are often visible, like sand or sawdust in water.

ask_qa.q: How can you tell the difference between a solute and a solvent in a liquid-liquid solution?
ask_qa.a: In a mixture of two liquids, the substance present in the smaller amount is the solute, while the one in the larger amount is the solvent.

ask_qa.q: Is there an exception to the rule that the liquid is always the solvent when mixing a solid and liquid?
ask_qa.a: Yes, the chapter mentions 'Chashni' (sugar syrup). Even though it contains a large amount of solid sugar and a small amount of water, water is still considered the solvent.

ask_qa.q: Common misconception: Does stirring a glass of tea allow more sugar to dissolve?
ask_qa.a: No, stirring only helps the solute dissolve faster by bringing it into contact with fresh solvent. It does not change the maximum amount (solubility) that the water can hold.

ask_qa.q: What is the difference between an unsaturated and a saturated solution?
ask_qa.a: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute at its current temperature, whereas a saturated solution has reached its limit and cannot dissolve any more.

ask_qa.q: Is it true that all substances become more soluble when you heat them?
ask_qa.a: No. While most solids increase in solubility with heat, the solubility of gases like oxygen actually decreases as the temperature of the water increases.

ask_qa.q: What is the difference between a dilute solution and a concentrated solution?
ask_qa.a: A dilute solution has a small amount of solute relative to the solvent, while a concentrated solution has a large amount. These are relative terms used to compare two solutions.

ask_qa.q: Common mistake: Are 'mass' and 'weight' the same thing?
ask_qa.a: No. Mass is the actual quantity of matter in an object (measured in grams/kilograms), while weight is the force of gravity pulling on that object (measured in Newtons).

ask_qa.q: Is it true that an object's density changes if you cut it into smaller pieces?

ask_qa.q: What is the difference between Density and Relative Density?

ask_qa.q: Why does a peeled orange sink while an unpeeled one floats?

ask_qa.q: Is it true that heating a substance makes it heavier?

ask_qa.q: How do you correctly read the meniscus of a clear liquid like water?

ask_qa.q: What happens to the density of a gas if you increase the pressure?
ask_qa.a: Increasing pressure packs the gas particles closer together, which decreases the volume and increases the density.

ask_qa.q: Is it true that pressure has a big effect on the density of solids and liquids?
ask_qa.a: No, the effect is negligible. Particles in solids and liquids are already very close together, making them nearly incompressible.

ask_qa.q: How does ice differ from liquid water in terms of density?
ask_qa.a: Unlike most substances, water expands when it freezes into ice. This larger volume means ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why it floats.

ask_qa.q: What is the 'displacement method' and when do we use it?

ask_qa.q: Is air considered a solution?

ask_qa.q: Why does hot air rise in a hot air balloon?

ask_qa.q: Is it true that sugar and salt dissolve in oil?

ask_qa.q: What is the difference between the density of the Earth's crust and its core?

ask_qa.a: Sand is denser than water, causing it to sink, while sawdust is less dense than water, which makes it float.

ask_qa.q: Why does an iron rod feel heavier than a wooden stick of the exact same size?
ask_qa.a: This happens because iron has a higher density, meaning there is more mass packed into the same unit of volume compared to wood.

ask_qa.q: How does increasing the temperature of a substance affect its density?
ask_qa.a: Heating usually causes particles to move apart and spread out, increasing the volume and thereby decreasing the density.

ask_qa.q: Why is the density of solids and liquids mostly unaffected by pressure?
ask_qa.a: Their particles are already very close together, making them nearly incompressible, so pressure has a negligible effect.

ask_qa.q: How is the volume of an irregular object like a stone measured?
ask_qa.a: It is measured using the displacement method, where the stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the rise in water level is recorded.

ask_qa.q: Why does ice float on top of liquid water?
ask_qa.a: When water freezes at 0 °C, it expands and the particles take up more space, making the ice less dense than the liquid water.

ask_qa.q: Why do hot air balloons rise in the sky?
ask_qa.a: Hot air is less dense than the cool air surrounding it, and this lower density causes it to move upward.

ask_qa.q: How can you make a sinking egg float in a glass of water?
ask_qa.a: By adding salt to the water, you increase the density of the liquid until it becomes greater than the density of the egg.

ask_qa.q: Why are measuring cylinders designed to be tall and narrow?
ask_qa.a: The narrow shape makes it easier to see small changes in volume and allows for more accurate readings of the liquid level.

ask_qa.q: How does the density of Earth's layers change as you move toward the core?
ask_qa.a: The density increases because higher pressure and temperature toward the center make materials heavier and more compact.

ask_qa.q: What happens to the density of a piece of modeling clay if you change its shape from a cube to a thin sheet?
ask_qa.a: The density remains the same because density is independent of shape; the ratio of mass to volume does not change.

ask_qa.q: Why were bamboo poles traditionally used to make rafts?
ask_qa.a: Bamboo is light, hollow, and less dense than water, which allows it to float easily and carry weight across water.

ask_qa.q: Why does an unpeeled orange float while a peeled one sinks?
ask_qa.a: The peel contains tiny air pockets that act like a life jacket to lower the orange's density; removing the peel makes it denser than water.

ask_qa.q: How should you read the volume of a clear liquid in a measuring cylinder?
ask_qa.a: You must place your eyes at the level of the curved surface and read the mark that coincides with the bottom of the meniscus.

ask_qa.q: Why does stirring not allow more salt to dissolve in a saturated solution?
ask_qa.a: Stirring only increases the speed of dissolving by bringing fresh solvent to the solute; it does not change the actual solubility limit.

ask_qa.q: How does the 'tare' button on a digital balance work?
ask_qa.a: It resets the reading to zero so you can ignore the mass of the container (like a watch glass) and only measure the object inside.

ask_qa.q: Why is relative density expressed without any units?
ask_qa.a: It is a ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water, so the units cancel each other out.

ask_qa.q: What happens to the volume of water when it turns into ice?
ask_qa.a: The volume increases because the particles arrange themselves into a structure that occupies more space.

ask_qa.q: How is the concentration of a solution determined?
ask_qa.a: It is determined by the amount of solute present in a fixed quantity of the solution or solvent.

ask_qa.q: What is the difference between a dilute and a concentrated solution?
ask_qa.a: A dilute solution has a smaller amount of solute, while a concentrated solution has a larger amount of solute in the same volume of solvent.

ask_qa.q: Why do some oil packets weigh less than 1 kg even if the volume is 1 litre?
ask_qa.a: This happens because the density of the oil is less than the density of water, meaning 1000 mL of oil has less mass than 1000 mL of water.

ask_qa.q: What is the key difference between a mixture and a solution for a Grade 8 student?
ask_qa.a: While all solutions are mixtures, only uniform (homogeneous) mixtures are called solutions because their components are evenly distributed and not visible separately.

ask_qa.q: In a solution of sugar and water, why does the sugar seem to disappear?
ask_qa.a: The sugar (solute) breaks down into tiny particles that spread evenly throughout the spaces between water particles (solvent), creating a uniform mixture.

ask_qa.q: How can you tell if a mixture is non-uniform just by looking at it?
ask_qa.a: In a non-uniform mixture, like sand in water, you can see the different components with your naked eye or a magnifying glass because they aren't evenly spread.

ask_qa.q: In liquid-liquid solutions, how do we decide which one is the 'boss' (solvent)?
ask_qa.a: We use the 'smaller amount' rule: the liquid present in the smaller quantity is the solute, and the one in the larger quantity is the solvent.

ask_qa.q: Why is 'Chashni' (sugar syrup) an exception to the 'larger amount is solvent' rule?
ask_qa.a: Even though there is more sugar than water, water is still the solvent because it is the liquid that does the dissolving of the solid solute.

ask_qa.q: What determines if a solution is 'saturated' at a specific temperature?
ask_qa.a: A solution is saturated when it has reached its limit and cannot dissolve any more solute; any extra added will just settle at the bottom.

ask_qa.q: If I have an unsaturated solution, can I add more solute?
ask_qa.a: Yes, an unsaturated solution has not yet reached its limit, so it can still dissolve more solute at that current temperature.

ask_qa.q: How can I make a saturated sugar solution dissolve more sugar without adding water?
ask_qa.a: You can heat the solution. For most solids, increasing the temperature increases their solubility, allowing the liquid to hold more solute.

ask_qa.q: Does stirring a glass of salt water actually increase the solubility of the salt?
ask_qa.a: No, stirring only helps the salt dissolve faster by bringing it into contact with fresh water; it does not change the total amount the water can hold.

ask_qa.q: Why do fish find it harder to breathe in very warm pond water?
ask_qa.a: The solubility of gases like oxygen decreases as temperature increases, so warm water contains less dissolved oxygen than cold water.

ask_qa.q: Is air considered a solution, even though it is made of gases?
ask_qa.a: Yes, air is a gaseous solution because it is a uniform mixture of different gases like nitrogen and oxygen that are evenly distributed.

ask_qa.q: What is the science behind why salt dissolves in water but not in cooking oil?
ask_qa.a: Water has a chemical nature that allows it to attract and break apart salt particles, whereas oil has a different structure that doesn't interact with salt the same way.

ask_qa.q: How can you distinguish between a dilute and a concentrated solution?
ask_qa.a: A dilute solution has a small amount of solute relative to the solvent, while a concentrated solution has a much larger amount of solute in the same volume.

ask_qa.q: If you break a piece of iron into two, does its density change?
ask_qa.a: No, density is a property of the material. Since both mass and volume decrease proportionally, the ratio (Mass/Volume) remains exactly the same.

ask_qa.q: Why is the SI unit for density kg/m³, but we often use g/mL in the school lab?
ask_qa.a: kg/m³ is the international standard, but g/mL is more convenient for small lab measurements because 1 mL of water has a mass of exactly 1 gram.

ask_qa.q: Why is Relative Density written as a pure number without any units like 'g' or 'mL'?
ask_qa.a: Relative density is a ratio of two densities (Substance Density / Water Density). Since the units are the same on top and bottom, they cancel each other out.

ask_qa.q: If an object has a relative density of 0.8, will it float or sink in water?
ask_qa.a: It will float because its relative density is less than 1, meaning it is less dense than water.

ask_qa.q: Why does a heavy wooden log float while a tiny iron nail sinks?
ask_qa.a: Floating depends on density, not weight. Wood is less dense than water, so even a heavy log floats, while iron is denser than water, so even a light nail sinks.

ask_qa.q: What is the 'displacement method' for measuring volume?
ask_qa.a: It involves submerging an irregular object in water and measuring how much the water level rises; the rise in volume is equal to the volume of the object.

ask_qa.q: When using a measuring cylinder, why must we look at the 'meniscus'?
ask_qa.a: The meniscus is the curve the liquid makes; for water, we must read the level at the bottom of the curve at eye level to get an accurate measurement.

ask_qa.q: Why are measuring cylinders tall and narrow instead of wide like a beaker?
ask_qa.a: The narrow shape makes the markings further apart, which helps us see even small changes in volume more accurately.

ask_qa.q: What happens to the density of air inside a hot air balloon when it is heated?
ask_qa.a: The heat causes the air to expand (increase volume), which decreases its density. This makes the balloon lighter than the cool air around it, so it rises.

ask_qa.q: Why does ice float on top of water instead of sinking to the bottom?
ask_qa.a: When water freezes, it expands and occupies more space. This increased volume makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

ask_qa.q: Why can't we compress a solid block to make it denser using normal pressure?
ask_qa.a: In solids, the particles are already packed very tightly together, so pressure has a negligible effect on their volume and density.

ask_qa.q: How does increasing pressure affect the density of a gas in a cylinder?
ask_qa.a: Increasing pressure forces the gas particles closer together, decreasing the volume and significantly increasing the density.

ask_qa.q: How can you make a sinking egg float in a glass of tap water?
ask_qa.a: Add salt to the water to increase the liquid's density. Once the water's density becomes higher than the egg's density, the egg will float.

ask_qa.q: What did Asima Chatterjee use solvents for in her scientific work?
ask_qa.a: She used solvents to extract and isolate important medicinal compounds from plants to develop drugs for malaria and epilepsy.

ask_qa.q: Why do the layers of the Earth get denser as you go deeper toward the core?
ask_qa.a: The materials toward the center are heavier and are packed more compactly due to the extreme pressure and temperature of the layers above.

ask_qa.q: What is the difference between mass and weight in a science lab?
ask_qa.a: Mass is the actual amount of matter in an object (in grams), while weight is the force of gravity pulling it down (in Newtons).

ask_qa.q: How do you 'tare' a digital balance, and why is it useful?
ask_qa.a: Taring resets the balance to zero after placing a container on it, so you only measure the mass of the substance inside, not the container itself.

ask_qa.q: If 1 mL equals 1 cm³, what is the density of 50g of a liquid that fills 50 mL?
ask_qa.a: The density would be 1 g/cm³ (50g / 50cm³), which is the same as the density of water.

ask_qa.q: How do we calculate the volume of a regular solid like a textbook?
ask_qa.a: We multiply its length, width, and height (L × W × H) using a ruler to find the total space it occupies in cubic centimeters.

ask_qa.q: Why was bamboo historically used for rafts in places like Manipur?
ask_qa.a: Bamboo is naturally hollow and light, making it much less dense than water, which allows it to float easily even when carrying weight.

ask_qa.q: What happens to the concentration of a salt solution if some water evaporates?
ask_qa.a: The concentration increases because there is now more solute (salt) relative to the smaller amount of solvent (water) left behind.

ask_qa.q: Is the mixture of gases in water (like oxygen) uniform or non-uniform?
ask_qa.a: It is a uniform mixture (a solution) because the gas particles dissolve and spread out evenly among the water particles.

ask_qa.q: What is the relationship between volume and density when mass stays the same?
ask_qa.a: They have an inverse relationship; if the volume increases (like when heating), the density must decrease.

ask_qa.q: Why is water often called a 'versatile' or 'good' solvent?
ask_qa.a: Water can dissolve a wide variety of substances, including solids (sugar), liquids (juice), and gases (oxygen), making it essential for life.

ask_qa.q: How does the 'Probe and Ponder' question explain the taste of ORS?
ask_qa.a: ORS tastes the same in every sip because it is a uniform solution where salt and sugar are evenly distributed throughout the water.

ask_qa.q: If a stone has a mass of 100g and displaces 20 mL of water, what is its density?
ask_qa.a: The volume is 20 cm³, so the density is 100g / 20cm³ = 5 g/cm³.

Water is one of the few substances on Earth that is less dense as a solid (ice) than as a liquid.
The Earth's layers are sorted by density—the lightest rocks are in the crust, while the heaviest metals are in the core.
Traditional salt wells in Manipur use 100-year-old tree trunks to draw up salty water for boiling.
Hot air balloons fly because the hot air inside is less dense than the cooler air outside, creating 'lift'.

chapter.title: How Nature Works in Harmony
chapter.summary: This chapter teaches us how living organisms and their non-living surroundings work together to create a balanced environment called an ecosystem. We explore how energy flows through food chains and webs, from producers like plants to decomposers like fungi that recycle nutrients. It also highlights the importance of human conservation efforts, such as protecting elephant corridors and practicing sustainable farming, to maintain nature's harmony.
key_points: A habitat is the specific place where an organism lives and finds everything it needs to survive.
Biotic components are the living parts of a habitat (plants, animals, microbes).
Abiotic components are the non-living parts (sunlight, air, water, soil, temperature).
A population is a group of the same type of organisms living together in one place.
A community consists of different populations of various species sharing the same habitat.
Producers (autotrophs) make their own food, while consumers (heterotrophs) eat other organisms.
Decomposers (saprotrophs) break down dead matter and return essential nutrients to the soil.
A food web is a network of interlinked food chains showing 'who eats whom' in an ecosystem.
Mutualism is a relationship where both organisms benefit, such as honeybees and flowers.
The Sundarbans are the world's largest mangrove forests and protect coastal areas from storms.
Sustainable farming avoids the overuse of synthetic chemicals to protect soil health and biodiversity.
Human-made ecosystems like farms and parks require active management to stay healthy.

In several parts of India, particularly in states like Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Assam, and Chhattisgarh, elephants often enter farms and villages. When vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry up in their natural habitat, elephants may wander into nearby farms or plantations in search of food like bananas and sugarcane. This can lead to crop damage and at times, even harm people and domestic animals. Changes in rainfall and temperature affect vegetation. Cutting down trees for constructing roads and buildings makes it worse. This leads to the drying and shrinking of forests, the natural home of animals. Because of loss of habitat, animals tend to move into human habitats. Elephants are adapted to forest life, but sudden changes make it hard for them to survive. Wildlife ecologists have identified  and marked corridors in many parts of the country to allow safe movement of animals. These corridors connect forest habitats, enabling wildlife—such as elephants to travel in need between large forest areas without coming into conflict with human settlements. This chain of events shows how closely nature’s elements are connected. To understand such interconnections, we must study the components of our environment.
12.1  How Do We Experience and Interpret

Our Surroundings? You have learnt in Curiosity, Grade 6 chapter ‘Diversity in the Living World’ that different habitats have different kinds of plants and animals. A habitat is simply place where an organism lives. It could even be just the bark of a tree. The plants and animals interact with each other and adapt to survive in the surrounding conditions they live in. Explore two nearby habitats and identify both the living organisms and the non-living components in each.
Activity 12.1: Let us explore
Caution: Explore the habitat in groups with your teacher.

z These could be any two of the following: a pond, a forest, an
agricultural farm, or even a large tree like banyan, mango, or pilkhan (white fig) tree.

in these habitats.

Pond Forest Living beings Non-living things Living beings Non-living things Fish Water Grass Soil Trees Birds

What common characteristics do you observe in the two habitats in
Activity 12.1? The similarities are that

both habitats have living beings as well as non-living things. However, the types of living beings are different and the non-living things also vary. The living beings you have recorded in Table 12.1 are termed as the biotic components and non-living things as the abiotic components of a habitat. Have you wondered why some organisms live on land while others live in water? Every organism needs specific conditions to survive. From this activity, you can see that different habitats offer different living conditions. In Activity 12.1, you listed fish as a biotic component of the pond. How do fish survive in a pond? A pond provides food, oxygen, shelter, and space to grow  — conditions essential for survival of organisms. Fish obtain their biotic needs, such as food, from small plants and animals, and abiotic needs, such as oxygen, from water. Other living beings also inhabit the pond, such as frogs, turtles, snakes, dragonflies, mosquitos, snails, and ducks, along with plants like algae, diatoms, duckweeds, and lotus. They all interact with the other living beings and non-living things present in the places where they grow and thrive. (a) Pond habitat
Fig. 12.1: Two types of habitats
(b) Forest habitat

Each habitat has its own biotic components and physical conditions — air, sunlight, water, temperature, and soil. Different organisms living in the same habitat may use the re sources in different ways. A forest might be warm during the day and cool at night. A snake that comes out at night and a rodent active during the day both live in the same habitat, but they face different conditions. This is how living organisms coexist in harmony in the same habitat.
12.2 Who All Live Together in Nature?

You have observed fish in a pond in Activity 12.1. Did you see only a single fish? Most likely, you may have seen many fish of the same kind. This group of fish of the same kind living together in a pond habitat is called a population of that particular fish. In this way, we can observe and record populations of different kinds of organisms in a single habitat.

From Activity 12.2, we can explain that the population is a group of the same type of organisms in a habitat at a given time. Can a habitat have only one type of living organism? What might happen then? If all organisms are the same, they would have the same requirements — food, water , space — leading to competition and possible scarcity of resources. What else do you think could happen? In Activities 12.1 and 12.2, you observed that different group of organisms live together in a habitat. A community comprises different populations sharing the same habitat. The biotic components of a habitat, such as the plants, animals, and microorganisms together form the community. These organisms interact and depend on one another for survival.
Ever heard of ...

You may have seen brightly coloured flowers blooming around you. Have you ever looked closely at their parts? A flower has a stalk, green leafy structures called sepals, coloured petals and two reproductive parts — Carpels (female) and stamens (male). Stamens burst and release yellow dust like pollen grains. Wind, water , insects, bats, and birds help carry pollen from the stamens to the carpels of the same and/or different flowers. This process is called pollination (Fig. 12.2). It is essential for the formation of fruits and seeds.

Matter? Let us find out the role of different organisms in a community.
Activity 12.3: Let us read
z Researchers conducted a study to see how fish in ponds
affect seed production in the plants nearby. They observed
Fig. 12.3: Pond A with fish and Pond B without fish
Pond A Pond B
two ponds — A with fish and large number of flowering plants around it; B without fish and fewer flowering plants around it (Fig. 12.3). Think of a reason for these observations.
z Compare the number of dragonflies,

bees, and butterflies in both the ponds. Do you find any relationship between the number of dragonflies and bees/butterflies? We observed that in Pond A (with fish) the number of dragonflies were less as compared to Pond B. Why?
z Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so ponds with fish

had fewer dragonflies. Dragonflies usually eat flies, bees and butterflies. With fewer dragonflies, more bees, flies, and butterflies were found. These insects help pollinate flowers from nearby areas moving pollen from one flower to another , which helps plants produce seeds. So, flowers near ponds with fish may produce more seeds than those near ponds without fish.
z What does this study show? How does the population of fish
in a pond affect the seed production in nearby plants?
z This study shows how biotic components (fish, dragonflies,

pollinators, plants) and abiotic components (temperature, water , nutrients) interact with and affect each other (Fig. 12.4). Similarly, can overfishing by humans change this balance? How do you think it may affect the living and non-living parts of the habitat?
12.4  What Are the Different Types of Interactions

Among Organisms and their Surroundings? In Curiosity, Grade 7, you learn about how plants and animals need air , water , soil, and sunlight to grow. Living organisms, or the biotic community, depend on non-living things, that is abiotic components for their survival. Plants and animals also depend on each other for nutrition, respiration, and reproduction. These are interactions among the biotic components. Both types of interactions  — among biotic components, and between biotic and abiotic components — are important for survival in any habitat.

In Activity 12.4, you understood different types of interactions  occur within a habitat. From this, you can infer that the biotic components (plants, animals, and microorganisms) and the abiotic components (air, water, soil, sunlight, and temperature) in a habitat interact with each other to form an ecosystem. Organisms in an ecosystem interact with abiotic components for food, shelter, and protection. Different communities of living organisms interact with abiotic components in an ecosystem. There are two main types of ecosystems in nature. Aquatic ecosystems include ponds, rivers, and lakes while terrestrial ecosystems include forests, farms or even large trees like banyan, mango, or pilkhan. Hence, ecosystems can be large or small. Can you find overlapping ecosystems in Fig. 12.6?
Fig. 12.6 shows an overlap of different terrestrial and

aquatic ecosystems. In this figure, you can see a small river (an aquatic ecosystem) along with mountains, forests, grassland, and farmland, which are examples of terrestrial ecosystems. Farmland is a human-made ecosystem. These ecosystems are interacting with each other at any given point. In Activity 12.4, we have seen the importance of the components and their interactions in an ecosystem. For example, sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water are essential for producing food in plants; soil provides medium and essential nutrients for plant growth; air provides oxygen for respiration in plants as well as animals; water is essential for all living organisms. This shows how living organisms depend on the non-living component of an ecosystem. Just as biotic components depend on abiotic components, abiotic components are also influenced by biotic components. For example, plants release oxygen during photosynthesis, roots hold soil in place and prevent erosion, and plants retain soil moisture and help cool the atmosphere. You can identify and study any ecosystem in your surroundings and observe different types of interactions among the biotic and abiotic components. While studying biotic interactions, notice how organisms depend on each other for food.

How do plants get their food? As you know, plants make their own food by the process of photosynthesis. Thus, they are called producers or autotrophs (auto=self + troph=food). Organisms that cannot produce their own food and depend on other organisms for their food are called consumers or heterotrophs (hetero = other + troph = food). List the heterotrophs from Table 12.4. Organisms that eat only plants are called herbivores, such as deer and hare. Those that eat only animals are carnivores, such as leopard. Organisms that eat both plants and animals are omnivores, such as crows, foxes, and mice.

You know that living organisms grow, perform many functions, develop, and die. During their life cycle, organisms produce a lot of waste, including dead matter and food waste.
12.6 What Happens to Waste in Nature?

You may have seen small umbrella-like structures, mushrooms, growing on dead plants or trees during the rainy season (Fig.  12.12). These are a type of fungi that grow on dead matter. Microorganisms like fungi and bacteria break down complex substances in dead plants and animals into simpler ones. This  process returns

You can also find tiny insects, such as beetles and flies, on animal droppings  — like elephant dung— as they help break it down and recycle nutrients, back into the environment. This process is called decomposition and the organisms carrying out the process are called decomposers or saprotrophs (sapro= rotten + trophs = food). Plants grow in soil and many of the nutrients in soil come from the decomposition process. Thus, decomposers play an important role in recycling nutrients. In nature, nothing is wasted  — everything is reused. Does nature really waste anything?

India is a country with diverse habitats and seasons. Many migratory birds fly thousands of miles and reach different habitats in India. They migrate from different parts of the world to avoid harsh climate, and in search for food. Birds not only enhance the aesthetics of those habitats but also play a significant role in keeping the balance in an ecosystem as pollinators or seed dispersers along the path they migrate. This way they link two habitats. These birds are predators of insect pests and help farmers to control pest populations, and indirectly help in healthy crop growth. Migratory birds, Demoiselle Crane visit the water body of Khichan village in Jodhpur district during the winter months. Do you know which birds in your area are seen only during winter? Collect postal stamps and covers of migratory birds released by the Indian Postal Department, and collect information about their place of origin and reasons for their migration to different localities in India and more. Showcase the postal stamps in your science laboratory/school library to popularise migratory birds.
12.7 How Does One Change Lead to Another?
Look at Fig. 12.13. It shows how one small change can lead to many others. For example, many plants in a pond start dying because of pollution. With fewer plants less oxygen will be

produced in water which will lead to a drop in the fish population in that water body. Reduction in fish population will have cascading effects and there will be less number of consumers in the pond. As a result, insects will increase in number. These insects will spread to nearby farmlands. This is how farmers will be compelled to use pesticides to grow their crops which may again adversely affect the environment. Further consequences may emerge in the form of other environmental issues. Plants die Less oxygen Fish die More insects Plants get damaged by pests

In the 1980s, India was a significant exporter of frog legs, especially of the Indian bullfrog (Hoplobatrachus tigerinus) (Fig. 12.14). This large-scale harvesting led to a decline in frog populations. Since frogs eat insects, their reduced numbers resulted in a rise in agricultural pests. This forced farmers to use more synthetic pesticides, which harmed the environment, soil and water quality, and affected the overall environmental and human health. The Government of India banned the export of frog legs to prevent further ecological damage. An ecosystem stays in balance when interactions among organisms and their environment keep populations and resources stable. This balance is dynamic, not fixed, and can be disrupted by natural or human-made changes.

Be a scientist

Asir Jawahar Thomas Johnsingh (A.J.T. Johnsingh) was a famous Indian wildlife biologist who helped us understand forest ecosystems through the eyes of animals. He was a pioneer in studying wildlife through modern tracking system. His research showed how predators like tigers and leopards rely on prey, such as deer and wild boar, while he was working in Bandipur National Park, Karnataka. He proved that a healthy prey population is key to predator survival. He inspired many youngsters to study wildlife and protect the forests and biodiversity of India.
12.9 What Are the Benefits of an Ecosystem?

We have learnt that biotic components and abiotic components of an ecosystem depend on each other and support various life processes. Humans also benefit from ecosystems. For example, forests provide fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber, and medicines. Similarly, aquatic ecosystems provide water and food. Ecosystems also offer aesthetic and recreational value. These support our well-being and shows how closely nature and humans are connected. However, when we overuse or misuse natural resources, we disturb the balance in nature. Now let us look at a real-life example of a threatened ecosystem — the Sundarbans.

The Sundarbans have the largest mangrove forests in the world. Located where the Ganges and Brahmaputra Rivers meet between India and Bangladesh, the Sundarbans’ forests and rivers are home to various flora and fauna, many of which are endangered. The Sundarbans protect us by slowing down strong winds and waves during storms and floods. The trees also absorb carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen. Because of its importance, The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) declared the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site in 1987. However , the Sundarbans (Fig.  12.17) are under a serious threat. Mangrove trees are being cut for fuelwood and farming. Illegal hunting and overuse of forest resources are a threat to the wildlife living there. Pollution from industrial waste and untreated sewage in rivers are also damaging the water and habitat. These human activities disrupt the natural way ecosystems work. Similarly, other ecosystems across India are also under threat. Problems like deforestation, overuse of natural resources, the spread of invasive species, unsustainable land use, and pollution are damaging forests, rivers, scrublands, wetlands, grasslands, and coastal areas. How can we stop damaging forests, rivers, and wetlands? Think about what actions you and your community can take to protect these important places. Protected areas are parts of land or water set aside to conserve wildlife and their habitats. India has many protected areas like national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, and community conserved areas. These places help protect entire habitats including endangered animals, birds, and many rare plants. Famous examples include Jim Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand), Manas National Park (Assam), Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (Western Ghats), Chilika Lake (Odisha), Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary (Arunachal Pradesh), Hemis National Park (Leh), Keibul Lamjao National Park (Manipur), Pirotan Island Marine National Park (Gujarat). Protected areas play a big role in saving nature for future generations.

12.9.1 Human-made ecosystems

Humans have created artificial ecosystems like fish ponds, farms, and parks to meet their needs. When well designed, these can help reduce pollution, support biodiversity, and provide recreational spaces for people. Unlike natural ecosystems, these need human care and management. 12.9.2 How do healthy ecosystems serve our farms?

Farming, a major livelihood in India, can become unsustainable if not managed well by applying environment friendly farming practices. Humans have been practising farming for thousands of years to grow food. As the population grew, our dependence on agriculture increased. Between 1950 and 1965, India faced a food crisis due to low crop production. In the mid-20th century, the use of tractors, machines, synthetic fertilisers, and pesticides helped increase food production. This period is known as the Green Revolution. However , these farming methods are now considered unsustainable because of the overuse of synthetic chemicals, excessive groundwater extraction, and growing only one type of crop for commercial gain. How do these practices harm both the environment and human health? Many scientists believe that overusing pesticides and growing the same type of crop repeatedly on the same land leads to soil degradation. Understanding ecosystems can help us adopt better and more sustainable farming practices.

Synthetic fertilisers and pesticides have played a vital role in improving crop production and helped countries like India become food secure. However, their long-term use can affect the environment and soil health. Overuse of synthetic fertilisers may reduce soil fertility by decreasing friendly microorganisms in soil and lowering organic matter (humus), which helps bind soil particles. Without enough humus, soil becomes prone to erosion. Also, it reduces the population of natural predators which ultimately increase the population of pests (Fig. 12.18). Heavy irrigation and repeated ploughing can also disturb soil organisms like earthworms and snails, which are important for maintaining ecological balance. Some pests may develop resistance to pesticides, making them difficult to control. Growing the same crop repeatedly, known as monoculture, can reduce biodiversity and affect pollinators, which are crucial for food production. To make farming more sustainable, some farmers are exploring organic and natural farming methods. These aim to reduce the use of synthetic fertilisers and support sustainable farming, with minimal interference in natural ecosystems. Based on your learning, what practices do you think can help farmers protect the soil, the environment, and our food security for the future? The ancient text Vrikshayurveda emphasises on soil health and nourishment. The text strongly advocates for the continuous nourishment of the soil through organic manure like Kunapa Jala (a liquid fertiliser made from animal and plant waste by the process of fermentation; that breaks complex substances into simpler ones) and other composted materials.
